title-group.article-title: Urban Sediment Cascade as Geochemical Archive: Tracking Industrial Impact and Pollution in Urban Environment

abstract.p: Urban surface deposited sediments are important reservoirs of pollutants, yet their relationships with other environmental media and their value for distinguishing legacy contamination from current anthropogenic inputs remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the urban sediment cascade across eight industrial cities in Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia. The study combines geochemical data for urban soils from regional monitoring with analyses of urban surface deposited sediments, their fine fraction (<0.1 mm), and snow cover. Concentrations of Mg, Mn, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd, Sb, and Pb in the sediment cascade strata were considered. An initial geochemical baseline was reconstructed using principal component analysis and non-parametric Kernel density estimation. Pollution was assessed using geochemically justified element-specific pollution index and an integrated toxicity-weighted pollution index. The multi-strata profiling and analysis of eco-geochemical spectra successfully isolated key trajectories of technogenic transformation, including post-industrial legacy, continuous metallurgical complexes pressure, mining impacts, and climate-dependent transboundary transit. The toxicity-weighted pollution assessment classified 54% of sampling sites as heavily or severely polluted. The developed approach provides a universally scalable methodology for multi-temporal environmental monitoring within industrial and post-industrial urban areas.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Over the past century, urbanization has emerged as a pivotal global trend. Currently, more than half of the world’s population is concentrated in urban agglomerations, with this figure reaching three-quarters in high-income countries [1]. The concentration of human capital and infrastructure renders cities hubs of innovation and development, while simultaneously transforming them into areas of concentrated environmental pressure [2,3,4]. The Sverdlovsk Oblast of Russia stands out as a region where this trend is particularly pronounced, with its urbanization level reaching 86% [5]. Notably, a significant proportion of this population resides in small cities [6].

The environmental impact of cities is all-encompassing, radically transforming natural landscapes [7,8,9]. Natural land surfaces are replaced or modified by artificial objects such as asphalt, concrete, lawns [10,11]. The hydrological network undergoes profound alterations: rivers are culverted, storm-water retention ponds are constructed [12,13,14], vegetative species composition is displaced, and fauna is modified [15,16,17,18]. Consequently, the urban landscape becomes a heterogeneous mosaic where natural and anthropogenic elements are closely intertwined [7,19,20,21].

Despite deep anthropogenic transformation, fundamental natural processes in cities do not cease but are merely modified. One such key process is sedimentation: the formation, transport, and accumulation of loose sedimentary material [13,22,23,24]. In urban environments, the weathering of bedrock is supplemented by the degradation and wearing of construction materials and road pavements, while soil erosion is exacerbated by the disruption of vegetative cover and soil compaction [11,19,25,26]. Consequently, urban sediment formation reflects the combined influence of natural processes and anthropogenic activities [9,12,27].

In urban environments, sedimentary material manifests in diverse forms depending on its accumulation site and particle size distribution. These include atmospheric particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5), a respirable fraction that poses a direct threat to the respiratory system [28,29,30,31,32]. Another form is road dust, which consists of coarse material on road surfaces enriched with anthropogenic particles [26,33,34]. Generally, urban surface deposited sediments (USDSs), which accumulate in micro-relief depressions, act as an integral geochemical barrier that intercepts pollutants from the local catchment area [27,35]. The uniqueness of the USDSs lies in their high heterogeneity and capacity for rapid transformation; upon drying, they become a major source of secondary atmospheric dust resuspension [7,36,37].

The accumulation of the USDSs entails a complex of negative environmental and socioeconomic consequences. Deposits can reduce the hydraulic capacity of stormwater drainage systems, contributing to localized flooding under conditions of intense precipitation [9,23,38]. Their removal also increases municipal street-cleaning costs, while abrasive particles may contribute to the wear of vehicles and machinery [9,38]. From an aesthetic perspective, mud and street dirt create an uncomfortable visual environment that is perceived negatively by residents, thereby reducing their overall quality of life [39]. Furthermore, these sediments contribute to the compaction of urban soils and a decline in their fertility [18,25].

Urban surface deposits pose a serious threat to human health, acting as vectors for both toxicants and pathogens. The greatest danger is associated with fine fractions that enter the human breathing zone during the deflation of dry sediment [29,32]. These particles contain heavy metals (e.g., Pb, Zn, Cu) [28,33,34,35], polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons [40,41], and microplastics [42], and their prolonged exposure is associated with an increased incidence of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. The spring snowmelt period is critical, as winter-accumulated pollutants [43,44,45] are released simultaneously (particle formation event [45]), generating peak stress on the immune systems of urban residents [46,47,48].

Because USDSs accumulate material from multiple sources, surface deposits serve as an informative indicator of the urban environmental status [40,49]. They accumulate pollutants from the atmosphere, soils, transport, and industries, thereby providing a time-integrated overview of the anthropogenic load. By examining the material and particle size composition of the sediment, source apportionment can be achieved (e.g., distinguishing lead from leaded gasoline, non-exhaust vehicle emissions, or metallurgical slag particles) [28,50]. In contrast to soils, which develop over centuries, or air quality, which fluctuates hourly, surface sediments provide a temporally stable signal of the geochemical transformation of the urban landscape over timescales ranging from a single season to several years.

Russian cities represent a specific, and in many aspects unique, object for studying sedimentary processes. First, the cold continental climate is characterized by a prolonged winter with a stable snow cover. Second, widespread use of studded tires (by up to 70–80% of vehicle owners) induce a distinctive winter sedimentogenesis that is absent in warmer regions of the world [24,48]. Third, the Soviet urban planning legacy, characterized by high housing density of residential districts with a deficit of parking spaces, provokes widespread illegal parking on lawns, which serves as a powerful source of topsoil erosion [7]. Fourth, many of the urban centers founded during industrialization era are “monocities” (a calque from the Russian monogorod), which describes a community heavily reliant on a single local industry. Such monocities generate distinct, highly localized geochemical anomalies [49,51].

Despite the obvious importance of contemporary urban surface deposits, comprehensive investigations into their material (mineralogical, chemical, and particle size) composition remain fragmented across many regions [52,53,54]. Most studies have focused either exclusively on the road dust or on the geochemistry of urban soils. Consequently, systematic data on how sediment composition varies depending on the urban functional zone (road vs. courtyard), season (summer vs. winter), climatic conditions, and geological baseline are highly limited. The standardization of sampling and sample preparation methods (e.g., the isolation of respirable fractions) presents a particularly critical issue. Without such a foundational understanding, establishing accurate pollutant migration models and developing effective urban dust mitigation measures remain impossible.

This study tests the hypothesis that the urban sediment cascade functions as a temporally stratified geochemical archive. The specific, testable expectations are that: (i) if the cascade preserves historical signatures, the legacy elements unique to past operations will be significantly enriched in stable strata (soils) rather than modern dynamic phases; and (ii) current industrial profiles will be distinctly captured by modern dynamic components (surface sediment, its fine fraction, and atmospheric deposition), showing chemically consistent loading patterns unique to each industry type (e.g., metallurgy vs. mining).

The investigation was conducted across eight industrial monocities within a single region, each characterized by the predominance of a specific industry and, consequently, a distinct pattern of anthropogenic impact.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Area
sec.p: Sverdlovsk Oblast is situated within the Middle and Northern Urals, partially extending into the West Siberian Plain. The administrative center of the region is the city of Ekaterinburg. The regional climate is continental, characterized by a prolonged, cold winter and a relatively warm summer. The mean temperature in January ranges from −13 to −20 °C, while in July it varies between +16 and +19 °C; a stable snow cover persists for an average of 150–180 days. Geologically, a substantial part of the region is confined to the Urals mountain system. The investigated cities are located within the following structural-formational zones of the Ural Orogen: the Tagil, East Ural, and Trans-Ural Megazones (Figure 1).

Sverdlovsk Oblast is one of the largest and oldest mining and industrial regions in Russia. Substantial reserves of ferrous and non-ferrous metal ores, combined with the historical development of the mining and metallurgical industries, have led to the formation of a powerful complex of extractive, metallurgical, machine-building, and chemical enterprises. Active industrial exploitation of the territory began in the 18th century, when working settlements began to emerge around metallurgical plants, many of which subsequently attained city status. Consequently, a distinctive anthropogenic landscape has developed in the region, where industrial activity serves as a key driver of the contemporary urban environmental quality.

The present study examines eight small- and medium-sized industrial cities within Sverdlovsk Oblast: Alapaevsk, Asbest, Verkhnyaya Pyshma, Kamensk-Uralsky, Kachkanar, Nevyansk, Pervouralsk, and Serov. These cities differ in their natural settings, topography, and, most importantly, industrial specialization, ranging from historical metallurgical centers to modern enterprises of non-ferrous and ferrous metallurgy and the mining industry.

Alapaevsk lies in the central-eastern part of Sverdlovsk Oblast, approximately 150 km northeast of Ekaterinburg. Founded in 1639, the city has a population of about 36,000 residents. Alapaevsk is situated on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, at the junction of the Trans-Ural Plain and the West Siberian Lowland, within the valley of the Neyva River. The topography is predominantly flat. The city is among the oldest industrial centers in the Urals and historically developed around metallurgical production. At the end of the 20th century, the local metallurgical plant ceased its operations. Currently, the primary industrial sectors are wood processing and the food industry.

Asbest is located in the eastern part of Sverdlovsk Oblast, on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals. The city emerged at the end of the 19th century due to the mining of the Bazhenovo chrysotile asbestos deposit and officially attained city status in 1933. The population is approximately 56,000 residents. The topography of the area is predominantly flat. The industrial specialization is rooted in the mining industry, primarily the extraction and processing of chrysotile asbestos, alongside the production of asbestos-technical products and construction materials. The largest industrial facility is the “Uralasbest” production association, whose core operations involve the exploitation of the Bazhenovo deposit and the processing of mineral raw materials.

Verkhnyaya Pyshma occupies a position within the suburban zone of Ekaterinburg, approximately 15 km north of the center of the city, on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals. Founded in 1854, the city has a population of about 74,000 residents. Situated in the upper reaches of the Pyshma River, the city features a predominantly hilly topography. Verkhnyaya Pyshma is a major center of non-ferrous metallurgy and the metalworking industry. The anchor enterprise “Uralelektromed” manufactures copper products.

Kamensk-Uralsky straddles the valleys of the Kamenka and Iset rivers in the southeastern part of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Founded in 1701, the city has a population of approximately 160,000 residents, making it the largest among the urban areas examined in this study. The topography is predominantly flat, locally dissected by river valleys. Currently, the city hosts large-scale pipe manufacturing alongside enterprises of ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy, machine-building, and metalworking. The largest industrial facilities include the Sinarsky Pipe Plant, the Metallurgical Plant, the Non-Ferrous Metal Working Plant, and the Urals Aluminum Smelter.

Kachkanar is located in the northwestern part of Sverdlovsk Oblast, at the foot of Mount Kachkanar. The city was founded in 1968 and has a population of approximately 37,000. It lies on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, within the watershed between the Isa and Viya rivers. The terrain is mountainous, characterized by substantial elevation differences. The city developed in association with the exploitation of the Kachkanar vanadium–titanium–magnetite deposit. Its industrial specialization is primarily based on iron ore extraction and beneficiation. The city-forming enterprise is the Kachkanar Mining and Processing Plant, which extracts ore in open-pit mines, processes it, and produces iron ore concentrate, sinter, and pellets. Open-pit mines, overburden dumps, and tailings storage facilities are also major sources of anthropogenic pressure.

Nevyansk lies in the central part of Sverdlovsk Oblast, on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, in the valley of the Neiva River. The settlement was founded in 1701 and now has a population of approximately 22,000. The terrain is predominantly flat to gently undulating. Nevyansk is one of the oldest mining and metallurgical centers in the Urals and historically developed around metallurgical production. At present, Nevyansk has no major industrial enterprises. However, the large Nevyansk Cement Plant is situated approximately 3 km southeast of the city. A further 9 km in the same direction lies the industrial town of Kirovgrad, which hosts the Kirovgrad Metallurgical Plant, an important non-ferrous metallurgical enterprise producing unrefined copper.

Pervouralsk is positioned on the western slope of the Ural Mountains, in the valley of the Chusovaya River, approximately 40 km west of Ekaterinburg. The city was founded in 1732 and has a population of approximately 110,000. The terrain is hilly and dissected by river valleys. Pervouralsk is a major hub for ferrous metallurgy, steel tube manufacturing, mechanical engineering, and silica refractory production. Its principal industrial assets include the Pervouralsk Pipe Plant and the Dinas Silica Refractory Plant. The city’s historical development was strongly associated with metallurgical production, resulting in a distinctly industrial landscape. In addition, the Middle Ural Copper Smelter is situated approximately 2 km away from Pervouralsk border. It is a major non-ferrous metallurgical enterprise in the Urals, specializing in copper smelting from primary raw materials and sulfuric acid production.

Serov is located in the northern part of Sverdlovsk Oblast, on the Kakva River. The city was founded in 1893 and has a population of approximately 93,000. It is situated at the boundary between the Middle and Northern Urals, on the eastern slope of the Ural Mountains. The terrain is predominantly flat, with several prominent uplands in the northern part of the city. Serov has historically developed as a major center of ferrous metallurgy. Its principal industrial facilities are the Nadezhdinsky Metallurgical Plant, which specializes in steelmaking and rolled metal production, and the Serov Ferroalloy Plant, a major producer of ferrochrome.

sec.title: 2.2.1. Urban Surface Deposited Sediment
sec.p: Following a previously described methodology [35,51], a composite sample of USDS was collected from 3–5 locations within each sampling site, including roadside areas, drainage ditches, and local micro-relief depressions within blocks of multi-story residential buildings and detached houses. A scoop and brush were used to collect the sediments, which were then transferred into polyethylene bags. The mass of each sample ranged from 1 to 1.5 kg. Figure 2 shows examples of USDS distribution across residential neighborhoods.

sec.title: 2.2.2. Snow Cover Sampling
sec.p: Sampling locations were selected in areas with undisturbed snow cover. Within blocks of multi-story residential buildings, such locations were typically situated in green spaces or playgrounds, as these areas are generally not used during the cold season. In detached house neighborhoods, snow samples were collected along the street-facing side of residential blocks, from green strips between private properties and roads or sidewalks. Sampling points were located 2–35 m from the road, at a mean distance of approximately 10 m.

Undisturbed snow cover was sampled using a dedicated snow sampler (Russian utility model patent No. RU 80587 U1). Sample collection and handling followed the procedures specified in the Guidelines for Atmospheric Pollution Monitoring (RD 52.04.186-89). The sampler consists of a plastic tube with a diameter of 10 cm and a piston that enables the entire snowpack profile to be recovered. Snow samples were collected in a 5 L sealable polyethylene container. The number of snow cores collected at each sampling location was determined by the container capacity. During sampling, the bottom portion of each core, including adhering surface material such as soil, leaves, and litter, was excluded from the sample. Snow samples were kept frozen during transportation and stored in an industrial freezer in the laboratory. Figure 3 shows examples of the snow cover sampled in this study.

sec.title: 2.2.3. Landscape Survey
sec.p: During sampling at each site, a landscape survey was performed to record the general characteristics of the site and the local catchment area, from which the mobilization of sedimentary material into the local micro-relief depressions occurred.

sec.title: 2.3. Chemical Analysis and Particle-Size Distribution
sec.p: The USDS samples were prepared in accordance with the Russian standard GOST 17.4.4.02-2017. Before analysis, coarse rock fragments, foreign materials, plant debris, and roots were removed from the samples. The material was then dried in a drying oven. Dry sieving through a 3-mm mesh was used to separate the >3 mm fraction, consisting predominantly of rock fragments, which was excluded from further analysis. The remaining fraction (<3 mm) was crushed using a rubber-tipped pestle and thoroughly homogenized.

A representative subsample was obtained by quartering and subsequently sieved through 1.0- and 0.1-mm meshes to separate the <0.1, 0.1–1, and 1–3 mm fractions. Each fraction was weighed using an analytical balance, and its mass percentage was calculated relative to the combined mass of the separated fractions. Representative subsamples of the <0.1 and 0.1–1 mm fractions were then pulverized to a particle size of 0.074 mm using an vibratory pulverizer prior to chemical analysis.

Particle-size analysis was performed on 10 randomly selected USDS samples from each city. Further analyses of the separated size fractions were conducted only on these 10 samples per city. The total elemental concentrations in the <0.1 mm fraction were determined for all samples.

Snow cover samples were prepared in accordance with GOST 31861-2012. The samples were thawed at room temperature for 24 h, after which coarse inclusions and plant debris were removed. The meltwater was filtered through ashless filters with a pore size of 0.002 mm using a vacuum filtration system. This procedure separated the snow samples into a suspended particulate fraction (>0.002 mm) and a filtrate (<0.002 mm). The suspended matter was air-dried at room temperature and subsequently subjected to elemental analysis.

Chemical analyses were performed at the Chemical Analytical Center of the Institute of Industrial Ecology UB RAS. The samples of USDS and snow cover samples were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) using an ELAN 9000 mass spectrometer (PerkinElmer, Shelton, CT, USA), in accordance with the Russian analytical procedure for determining the mass fractions of elements in solid materials (PND F 16.1:2.3:3.11-98). The detection limits for the solid phase were >5 mg/kg for Zn and Mg, >0.1 mg/kg for Mn, Ni, Cu, Sb, and Pb, and >0.05 mg/kg for Cd. Elemental concentrations in the liquid phase of the snow samples were determined by ICP-MS (ELAN 9000, PerkinElmer, CT, USA) using the same instrument, in accordance with the validated analytical procedure NSAM 480-X. The detection limits for the liquid phase were <2 μg/L for Ni, Cu, and Zn, <0.2 μg/L for Mn and Pb, and <0.1 μg/L for Cd and Sb.
Due to contamination of sieved samples by stainless steel abrasion particles, Cr is excluded from the analysis.

To assess the average rate of atmospheric pollutant deposition over the observation period, the accumulation of pollutants in the snow cover was calculated (mg/m2 per day). This parameter represents the rate at which elements accumulate within the snow cover over the period between snow accumulation and complete snowmelt:(1)AD=CMess·msample+CMeliq.ph.·VsampleNcores·Ssampler·Ndays, where AD is the atmospheric deposition of element, mg/m2 per day; Css and Cliq.ph. are the element concentrations in the suspended solids (mg/kg) and liquid phase (mg/L), respectively; msample is the mass of the suspended solids, kg; Vsample is the volume of meltwater, L; Ncores is the number of snow cores collected, pcs.; Ssampler is the area of the sampler, m2; and Ndays is the duration of snow cover accumulation, days.

For the atmospheric deposition of element in the snow cover, the lowest mean value observed across the surveyed cities was used as the background value. During winter, under conditions of persistent snow cover, local geochemical conditions are assumed to exert a substantially weaker influence on background atmospheric deposition. The background deposition is considered to be primarily associated with the weathering of building materials, road traffic, and domestic activities. Differences among the study cities in terms of these factors are assumed to be relatively minor.

Snow cover accumulation periods were determined using archived historical weather data obtained from SYNOP-coded weather reports available on the Pogoda i Klimat reference and information portal [55]. The accumulation period was established separately for each city (Table 1). The start date was defined as the date after which no further melting of the accumulated snow occurred, while the end date corresponded to the snow sampling date in each city.

sec.title: 2.4. Geochemical Data Considered in the Analysis
sec.p: A detailed analysis of the mineral composition of USDS was conducted previously. The results showed that each city develops a distinctive mineral assemblage in its sediments over time that is genetically associated with the local lithogenic substrate and the construction materials used in the urban environment [56]. This mineralogical complexity, reflecting multiple sources and formation processes, determines the characteristic baseline elemental composition of the sediments, their geochemical associations, and the background geochemical conditions of the urban environment. These factors must be taken into account when calculating environmental and geochemical indices.

Principal component analysis (PCA) of metal concentrations (Figure 4) identified three principal components that collectively explain 74% of the total variance. Most elements form two distinct, oppositely oriented clusters that contribute predominantly to the first principal component (PC1): one comprising Ce, La, Rb, Th, and U, and the other comprising Fe, V, and Ti. The second principal component (PC2) is characterized by opposing associations of Ni–Mg and Al–Sr. The third principal component (PC3) is associated primarily with variations in Mn concentrations.

Samples collected from cities belonging to different structural zones form largely non-overlapping clusters in principal component space. Samples from cities within the Tagil megazone plot in the field associated with ultramafic rocks of the lower continental crust and are diametrically opposed to samples from cities in the Trans-Ural megazone, which are associated with felsic rocks of the upper continental crust. Samples from cities in the East Ural megazone occupy an intermediate position between these two groups.

sec.title: 2.5. Estimation of the Initial Geochemical Baseline for the Urban Sediment
sec.p: To evaluate the initial geochemical baseline (IGB), the baseline relationship between the metal concentration Me and the scores of the first principal component PC1, associated with the content of major typomorphic elements, was reconstructed from the empirical data.
The function Me0(PC1), which approximates the IGB, was reconstructed based on the elemental composition of the sampled sediment cores under the following assumptions:
The baseline relationship Me0(PC1) is assumed to be linear, expressed as: Me0 = a + b∙PC1.

A fraction p of the collected samples represents geochemically undisturbed (uncontaminated) blanks. For these samples, the random deviations Δ = Me − Me0 are driven by natural variability and follow a symmetric normal distribution with a zero mean (M[Δ] = 0).

The remaining fraction of the samples (1 − p) is affected by an additional (anthropogenic) metal input MeP > 0, yielding a total concentration of Me(PC1) = Me0(PC1) + MeP. The value of MeP follows an asymmetric, right-skewed distribution (e.g., lognormal or exponential).
Under this model, when the true parameters a and b are identified, the continuous probability density function of the residuals, f(Δ), must reach its global maximum (mode) precisely at Δ = 0.
The optimization of the Me0(PC1) equation parameters was performed using an iterative local optimization approach:
The initial parameter approximations were established based on the average metal concentrations in the upper continental crust [57];

The continuous probability density function of Δ was estimated via non-parametric Kernel Density Estimation with a fixed bandwidth (for this analysis, the bandwidth was calculated based on the N—number of neighboring observations, where N is the total number of observations);
The target coefficients a and b correspond to the position where the global peak of the residual density distribution Δ is achieved at the zero point.

A limitation of this approach is that for certain metals, undisturbed samples may be predominantly concentrated within specific cities among the eight surveyed locations. Furthermore, pooling the datasets from different cities potentially offsets the localized variations in IGB across these urban areas. Baseline estimation was performed for the entire dataset and separately for each structural–formational megazone. The two approaches were compared to determine whether pooled or megazone-specific baseline estimation was more appropriate. For this purpose, deviations in the pollution index calculated using regional and pooled baselines were assessed. When the differences were negligible, the pooled approach was preferred because it was based on a larger number of samples and was therefore considered more robust.

sec.title: 2.6. Pollution and Toxicity Assessment
sec.p: The following indices were used to assess the degree of pollution and compositional transformation of USDSs.

sec.title: 2.6.1. Pollution Index (PI)
sec.p: The Pollution Index (PI) is a simple ratio of the measured concentration of an element to its background concentration and is calculated for each element in a sample [58,59]:(2)PI=CiCbg, where Ci is the concentration of element i in the sample, mg/kg, and Cbg is the background concentration of that element, mg/kg.

sec.title: 2.6.2. Nemerow Pollution Index (NPI)
sec.p: The Nemerow pollution index (NPI) [60] was used to assess the overall level of multi-element contamination in USDSs. The index combines the average and maximum PI, thereby accounting for both the cumulative contribution of the investigated elements and the influence of the most contaminated element. It was calculated as follows:(3)NPI=PIavg2+PImax22 where PIavg is the arithmetic mean of the PI for all investigated elements, and PImax is the maximum PI among these elements.

sec.title: 2.6.3. Toxicity-Weighted Pollution Index (TWPI)
sec.p: To assess the potential toxicity associated with USDS contamination in the surveyed cities, the toxicity-weighted pollution index (TWPI) was calculated. The index incorporates the mean PI values for individual elements and their respective hazard classes according to Russian sanitary regulations documents, established for soils and ambient air in populated areas. TWPI was calculated for each sample using the following equation:(4)TWPI=∑(PIi·Wi)∑Wi, where Wi is the weighting factor assigned to metal i.

Under the Russian sanitary regulations, metals are classified into four hazard classes according to their toxicological properties, with Class I representing the highest hazard [61]. The following weighting factors were assigned: 55 for Pb and Cd (Class I for both ambient air and soil); 33 for Zn (Class II for ambient air and Class I for soil); 20 for Cu and Ni (Class II for both ambient air and soil); 7.4 for Sb (Class III for ambient air and Class II for soil); 7.4 for Mn (Class II for ambient air and Class III for soil); and 2.7 for Mg (Class III for ambient air, based on MgO; not regulated for soil).
TWPI values were interpreted using the classification scheme applied to the NPI [60].

sec.title: 2.7. Regional Soil Monitoring Data
sec.p: This study used official data from the state environmental monitoring system on heavy metal contamination in soils. The Ural division of Russian Federal Service for Hydrometeorology and Environmental Monitoring (Roshydromet) periodically collects soil samples in various cities across Sverdlovsk Oblast. Samples are collected from the undisturbed upper soil horizon along compass bearings radiating from major pollution sources, at varying distances from these sources. Background soil samples are also collected. The analyses determine acid-soluble forms of the metals investigated in the present study, with the exception of Sb, Mg, and Mn.

The mean results of soil contamination assessments for the surveyed cities are regularly published in Roshydromet’s annual reports [62,63,64,65]. Of the eight cities included in this study, soil surveys of this type were conducted in seven: Kachkanar in 2009, Alapaevsk in 2011, Nevyansk in 2021, Verkhnyaya Pyshma and Kamensk-Uralsky in 2022, and Asbest and Pervouralsk in 2024. No comparable surveys were conducted in Serov.
For the present study, the PI was calculated as the ratio of the mean concentration of each metal to its concentration in the corresponding background soil samples.

sec.title: 3. Results
sec.p: A total of 300 USDS samples and 80 samples of undisturbed snow cover were collected from eight monocities. Landscape survey information was documented at all sampling sites. Particle-size distribution, chemical and mineralogical compositions were analyzed.

sec.title: 3.1. Characteristics of the Sampling Sites
sec.p: Figure 5 shows the mean contribution of different urban landscape functional zones to the area of surfaces surrounding each sampling site where USDSs were collected. These surfaces effectively constitute the catchment area from which sediment material was generated and transported to the sampling location. The results confirm the pronounced spatial heterogeneity of the urban landscape. They also suggest that USDSs comprise a mixture of particles originating from different parts of the surrounding area. Consequently, unlike road-deposited sediments, USDSs may provide a representative record of material derived not only from roads but also from other types of urban surfaces.

sec.title: 3.2. Results of Chemical Analysis
sec.p: Table 2 presents, for each city, the mean concentrations of the analyzed metals in USDSs, the ratios of metal concentrations in the fine fraction of USDSs to their mean concentrations, metal concentrations in the particulate fraction of snow cover, and the corresponding atmospheric depositions.

sec.title: 3.3. Cluster Analysis
sec.p: Table 3 presents element associations with correlation coefficients (r > 0.7) identified by cluster analysis of USDSs and snow cover samples from the surveyed cities. The analysis revealed a consistent Mg–Ni association across all cities and both media. In USDSs, the associations were predominantly limited to pairs and triplets of elements involving Zn, Pb, Cd, Cu, and Sb in various combinations. Snow cover samples exhibited a greater number of multielement associations. Mn was associated with potentially contaminant elements only in Serov.

sec.title: 3.4. Estimation of Geochemical Baseline
sec.p: Comparison of PI values calculated using the pooled baseline and megazone-specific baselines showed that stratifying the dataset by structural–formational megazones had a limited effect on the resulting PI estimates, with mean differences not exceeding 15%. Therefore, the dataset was not stratified by structural–formational megazones when deriving baseline relationships.

The reconstructed relationships between the IGB and PC1 scores are shown in Figure 6. For all metals, the parameters of the linear relationship could be optimized to produce a clearly defined maximum in the probability density function f(Δ) of the residuals (red line in Figure 6). As shown in Figure 6, the IGB line (black) passes through the region of low metal concentrations, whereas deviations from this line toward higher concentrations produce a right-skewed distribution with a tail extending toward higher values. The greater the deviation of a data point above the IGB line, the higher the inferred degree of contamination.

Figure 6 also shows that the cities differ both in the position of their data-point clouds along the PC1 axis, which reflects the geochemical characteristics of the underlying lithological substrate, and in the proportion of contaminated samples and the intensity of contamination attributable to anthropogenic impacts.

The reconstructed linear relationships Me0 = a + b∙PC1, are presented in Figure 6. The slope coefficient (b) varies among metals. Pb, Zn, Sb, Cd, and Ni exhibit positive relationships b > 0, consistent with the behavior of incompatible elements across the igneous rock differentiation series from mafic to felsic compositions. Magnesium exhibits the opposite trend, with concentrations decreasing as magmatic differentiation proceeds, as expected given its geochemical properties. The inverse relationship observed for Mn may be associated with the structure of the PCA results, particularly the fact that Mn loads predominantly on a separate principal component. The estimated background concentrations of Cu are approximately uniform across the surveyed cities and structural formations. In the inset in Figure 6, the line perpendicular to the IGB represents a common scale of anthropogenic enrichment applicable across all cities.

The estimated mean background concentrations of metals in USDS for the surveyed cities, together with the mean PC1 score for each city, are presented in Table 4. As shown in Table 4, the estimated background concentrations differ to some extent from the corresponding upper continental crust (UCC) values, which are commonly used as reference values for calculating pollution indices when site-specific background concentrations have not been established. The ranges of background concentrations in soils reported by the Ural division of Roshydromet generally encompass the IGB estimates for USDS. Notable exceptions include Mn in cities with PC1 >0 and Ni in all surveyed cities. The elevated Ni concentrations in background USDS samples may be associated with the use of serpentinite crushed stone in road and driveway construction [56].

sec.title: 3.5. Ecological and Geochemical Profiles
sec.p: Figure 7 presents the ecological and geochemical profiles of the eight cities, based on four sets of PI values: soil PI (for five metals across seven cities, based on Roshydromet data); USDS PI for the total fraction; USDS PI for the <0.1 mm fraction; and PI for atmospheric depositions, assessed using snow cover samples.

Soil is assumed to act as a long-term reservoir, accumulating pollutants over extended periods since the formation of the urban landscape. In contrast, given the deposition and removal rates reported in [24], USDS are estimated to have a mean age of approximately 2.5 years, with material older than 5 years accounting for no more than 12% of the total. This suggests that the magnitude of PI values for individual metals, media, and cities reveals patterns associated with the conditions of anthropogenic contamination in the urban environment, reflecting historical contamination, the cumulative effects of past and ongoing pollution, and current pollution trends. Elevated soil PI values indicate long-term contamination accumulated over several decades, as the sampling protocol specifies the collection of samples from undisturbed soil sites. By contrast, metal accumulation in USDSs reflects inputs over a period of several recent years. PI values for the fine USDS fraction reflect anthropogenic inputs associated with metals retained on the surfaces of fine particles. Atmospheric deposition, as assessed from snow cover, characterizes the current input of metals into the urban environment. Information on contamination is conveyed not only by the magnitude of individual PI values but also by the relative patterns of PI values across metals, media, and cities.

As shown in Figure 7, Alapaevsk exhibits evidence that substantial sources of anthropogenic contamination were previously present in the city: soil PI values for Pb, Cu, and Zn exceed those for the total USDS fraction and are approximately comparable to those for the fine fraction. For most metals, PI values in USDSs exceed those associated with current atmospheric deposition. High PI values for Mn and other metals are markers of residual environmental contamination resulting from the operation of the metallurgical enterprise. Current levels of anthropogenic contamination are minimal. Atmospheric deposition of Sb, Cu, and Zn apparently reflects current traffic-related pollution.

The main sources of contamination in Asbest are associated with the operation of the open-pit mine and mining and processing plant, which produces chrysotile asbestos and serpentinite crushed stone. PI values across the different media are relatively similar. The patterns of input and accumulation of Sb, Cu, Zn, and Cd reflect the current impact of road traffic.

In Nevyansk, the most notable feature is the high current atmospheric deposition of Pb, Sb, Cu, Zn, and Cd. The nearest source of anthropogenic inputs is the Kirovgrad Metallurgical Plant, located approximately 9 km southwest of the center of Nevyansk. An additional analysis of meteorological data showed that southwesterly winds prevailed during the winter of 2024–2025, when snow samples were collected, whereas the long-term mean winter wind direction is westerly. It can be assumed that the Kirovgrad Metallurgical Plant has some impact on the environmental conditions in Nevyansk, but this impact was less intensive in previous years. Nevyansk also exhibits the highest Mg deposition among the surveyed cities, which may be associated with the operation of the large cement plant on the outskirts of the city. The high snow pH of 10 also supports this interpretation.

Serov exhibits a complex pattern of environmental contamination, with indicators of both current and historical pollution. Anthropogenic impacts are associated with the operation of a large metallurgical enterprise that encompasses a wide range of technological processes, including iron ore sintering, blast-furnace ironmaking and slag accumulation, electric arc furnace steelmaking, and steel rolling. These activities are associated with substantial current inputs and contamination of USDSs by Pb, Cu, Zn, Cd, and Mn. The current deposition of Mg is apparently associated with increased MgO emissions from the Serov Ferroalloy Plant during the corresponding period. It can be assumed that Sb accumulated in the urban environment as a result of high-ash coal combustion at the power plant in previous years (before 2018) and is currently not present in atmospheric deposition in large quantities.

In Kachkanar, the main sources of contamination are dust emissions from overburden dumps and tailings storage facilities associated with the mining and processing plant. Mineral dust contains relatively low concentrations of heavy metals, as reflected in the low PI values for soils and USDSs. However, the study revealed relatively elevated PI values in snow cover, indicating increased current inputs. At present, these inputs cannot be attributed to any specific source. It should be noted that Kachkanar exhibited the highest dust load, averaging 163 mg/m2 per day [66].

A distinctive feature of Pervouralsk is that, in addition to its major metalworking and chromium alloy production facilities, the city is situated near one of the largest non-ferrous metallurgical enterprises in the region, a copper smelter. The ecological and geochemical profile of Pervouralsk clearly reflects the predominant impact of the copper smelter on the environment. High levels of current atmospheric deposition reflect, on the one hand, increased production in recent years and, on the other, insufficient efficiency of emission treatment. In this respect, the situation in Pervouralsk resembles that in Nevyansk. High concentrations of Cu and other heavy metals in USDSs and soils indicate substantial accumulated environmental damage.

The ecological and geochemical profile of Kamensk-Uralsky indicates the least pronounced contamination among the surveyed cities. For all the heavy metals and environmental media considered, PI values do not exceed 5 and, in most cases, remain below 2. This profile appears to be shaped primarily by road traffic. The local industrial sector is distinguished by the absence of mining and ferrous metallurgy, while non-ferrous metallurgy is represented by the aluminum industry. The main pollutants associated with aluminum production, including fluorine and other substances, are not heavy metals and are therefore not reflected in the sediment cascade examined in the soil–USDSs system.

In Verkhnyaya Pyshma, the elemental contamination profile (Sb, Pb, and Cu) clearly indicates inputs from a non-ferrous metallurgical enterprise. The city exhibits exceptionally high Cu deposition into the urban environment and the highest level of Cu accumulation in the fine USDS fraction. The relatively low levels of environmental contamination by Zn, Cd, Ni, Mn, and Mg may be explained by the fact that the enterprise does not process ore but instead processes blister copper and scrap metal.

sec.title: 3.6. Toxicity-Weighted Pollution Index
sec.p: Figure 8 shows the TWPI and NPI values, calculated using Equation (3) and (4) and based on the mean PI values for the USDSs for each city. The cities are ranked by TWPI. As shown in Figure 8, the highest TWPI values for the urban sediment occur in Serov and Pervouralsk (TWPI > 3, indicating severe pollution). In Alapaevsk and Verkhnyaya Pyshma, TWPI values range from 2 to 3, corresponding to heavy pollution. The lowest TWPI values are observed in Kachkanar, Kamensk-Uralsky, Nevyansk, and Asbest, ranging from 1 to 2 and indicating moderate pollution. Principally, there is a noticeable correlation between the integrated indexes TWPI and NPI, with the exception of the values for Asbest. In this city, the high PI values for Mg and Ni elevate the NPI, while in TWPI estimations, Mg is factored in with the lowest weight due to its low toxicity.

Figure 9 shows the distribution of sampling sites by TWPI pollution categories in the surveyed cities. Across the small industrial cities studied, 24% of all sampling sites fall into the severe pollution category and 30% into the heavy pollution category. Thus, more than half of the sampled sites fall into these two categories. The most unfavorable situation is observed in Serov, where 78% of sampling sites are classified as severely polluted. In half of cities, more than 50% of sampling sites fall into the heavy and severe pollution categories.

sec.title: 4.1. Conceptual Validation of Sediment Cascade as Multi-Temporal Environmental Archive
sec.p: The results obtained in this study fully confirm the proposed hypothesis that the components of the sediment cascade function as coupled geochemical archive with varying temporal depths, thereby allowing for the effective differentiation of legacy pollution from the current anthropogenic load. Combined analysis of eco-geochemical spectra (the relationship of PI across different environmental media and metals) successfully revealed the several distinct trajectories of technogenic transformation and ecological vulnerability in the investigated monocities: post-industrial legacy, continuous pressure from metallurgical complexes, impacts of mining activities, and transboundary atmospheric transport.

Alapaevsk provides a classic example of the post-industrial legacy trajectory. The closure of the city-forming metallurgical plant at the end of the 20th century led to a reduction in contemporary atmospheric deposition down to background levels. Nevertheless, critically high PI values in soils, coupled with the moderate heavy metal (Mn, Pb, Cu) enrichment of the USDSs, capture the phenomenon of a long-lived “geochemical memory” within urban ground substrates. The case of Alapaevsk clearly demonstrates that the cessation of industrial activity does not result in the instantaneous self-purification of environmental systems; rather, the legacy environmental footprint continues to be preserved within the solid phase of the cascade for decades. Conversely, in Nevyansk, where the destruction of the historical metallurgical core occurred more than a century ago, the self-purification of the soil cover is virtually complete. However, the current environmental situation there is complicated by high contemporary deposition driven by external factors.

In cities experiencing long-term, continuous industrial pressure (Pervouralsk, Verkhnyaya Pyshma, and Serov), the hypothesis is substantiated by synchronously high pollution levels across all strata of the accumulative and transport media cascade. Extreme peaks of copper accumulation in Verkhnyaya Pyshma and Pervouralsk, captured in both long-term (soil) and instantaneous (snow) profiles, reflect the ongoing intense impact of non-ferrous metallurgical enterprises. For Pervouralsk, these data find independent validation in multi-year bioindication and soil-ecological studies conducted by the Institute of Plant and Animal Ecology of UB RAS within the impact zone of the Middle-Ural Copper Smelter [67,68,69]. In Serov, a parallel increase in PI values for the USDS and snow deposition across a wide range of metals further attests to the sustained intensity of the local technogenic impact.

Residential areas of Asbest and Kachkanar experience constant environmental pressure driven by the exploitation of large-scale deposits and the operations of mining and processing plants (GOKs). The specific nature of environmental transformation in these cities lies in the dominance of lithophile elements rather than typical technogenic heavy metals. In Asbest, this is manifested in elevated Mg and Ni concentrations, which are directly linked to the mining of the Bazhenovo chrysotile asbestos deposit rich in serpentine. The mineral matrix of serpentinites, Mg3Si2O5(OH)4, is inherently characterized by extremely high crustal abundances of isomorphic Mg and associated Ni. In Kachkanar, the activities of the mining and processing complex operating on titanomagnetite ores are reflected in high contents of lithophile V, Fe, Ti, and Sc in atmospheric deposition, accompanied by an extreme physical dust load [66].

Significant pollution of the urban environment resulting from the long-range atmospheric transit of pollutants from neighboring industrial centers is recorded in Nevyansk and Pervouralsk. The situation in Nevyansk vividly demonstrates the high sensitivity of the upper strata of the sediment cascade to meteorological variations. Despite relatively low PI values in long-term accumulative media (soils), an extreme peak of current atmospheric deposition (snow) of Pb, Sb, Cu, Zn, and Cd was detected here during the 2024–2025 winter period. This anomaly, caused by a temporary shift in the plume direction from the Kirovgrad Metallurgical Plant under the influence of an atypical southwestern wind, proves that the upper stratum of the cascade (the snow cover) is capable of rapidly responding to synoptic and climatic fluctuations in atmospheric circulation. In Pervouralsk, the key pollution source is also formally situated outside the city’s municipal borders, albeit in close proximity. Obviously, for industrialized regions, accounting for transboundary atmospheric transport is a mandatory prerequisite when designing environmental monitoring programs and managing environmental quality. Furthermore, such monitoring programs require regular updating to align with contemporary climate.

It is essential to emphasize that the end-to-end analysis of the cascade also revealed the limits of the proposed method’s applicability. For instance, in Kamensk-Uralsky, which should be classified as a city under permanent industrial pressure based on its industrial structure, the standard analysis of heavy metal contents within the cascade failed to clearly identify tracers of local industrial impact. The results show that to unlock the environmental indicator potential of the sediment cascade under such specific conditions, it is necessary to expand the range of analyzed components and parameters by incorporating markers of the aluminum industry, primarily fluorine and bulk aluminum.

Characteristically, a background geochemical signal associated with vehicle operation is omnipresent across all the investigated cities. Effectively isolating traffic emissions against the backdrop of intense industrial inputs from active metallurgical giants is inherently impossible using simplistic monitoring techniques. Nevertheless, the case of Kamensk-Uralsky, which is relatively “clean” in terms of technogenic heavy metal loads, demonstrates that traffic-related contamination of the sediment cascade is characterized by the moderate accumulation of exhaust and non-exhaust emission elements (Sb, Pb, Cu, Zn, and Cd) at PI levels ranging from 2 to 3. These pollutants are predominantly localized within the upper soil horizon and the fine fraction of the USDSs, which aligns completely with findings reported worldwide [26,52,70,71,72].

Overall, an isolated analysis of a single component (such as studying exclusively soils or road dust alone), as practiced in many studies, leads to the loss of a crucial temporal context. The end-to-end, multi-strata profiling approach developed in this research, encompassing soil, bulk USDSs, the fine dust fraction of deposits, and snow cover, goes beyond merely stating the fact of contamination; it enables the clear separation of long-term legacy environmental footprints from the current technogenic inputs. This methodology has proven effective for forecasting environmental risks in an era of climate instability, which is of critical importance for modern environmental management.

sec.title: 4.2. Local Geochemical Baseline Framework
sec.p: One of the central strata of the examined accumulative and transport cascade—urban surface deposits—inherently lacks a predefined, pristine state. It is impossible to locate genuine urban sediment outside the urban environment, completely beyond the zone of technogenic impact, whereas within the city, deposits are invariably subjected to the combined effects of vehicular traffic, industrial facilities, and construction activities. Consequently, the chemical composition of these sediments cannot be directly compared against the chemical spectrum of a traditional background control site. In such scenarios, researchers conventionally rely on the global upper continental crust abundances [57]; however, this frequently introduces significant bias into the assessment of urban soils and sediments. As demonstrated on the example of monocities, the model based on Kernel Density Estimation consistently isolates the geogenic signal driven by the substrate transition from felsic to mafic rocks across diverse urban areas within the region. This framework enables the direct comparison of cities characterized by contrasting geological foundations (such as Kachkanar and Alapaevsk) on a unified scale of anthropogenic enrichment.

sec.title: 4.3. The Pervasive Mg–Ni Association: Infrastructure-Driven Homogenization of Urban Sediments
sec.p: Cluster analysis of the elemental composition of accumulative media has recorded a consistent strong correlation between Mg and Ni across all eight investigated monocities and within all strata of the sediment cascade. While Mg as a macroelement is conventionally associated with mafic and ultramafic rocks, this association is consistently reproduced not only in cities situated on an ultramafic bedrock foundation (Kachkanar, Pervouralsk) but also in territories characterized by felsic or sedimentary types of host rocks (e.g., Alapaevsk). This spatial uniformity indicates that the Mg–Ni pair is not of local industrial origin but rather possesses a regional-scale technogenic-infrastructure nature. The primary driving factor behind this specific regional trend is the widespread application of serpentinite crushed stone derived from the tailings of the Bazhenovo deposit as one of the primary road-construction materials throughout the entire region [56].

Intense mechanical abrasion of the road pavement by vehicular traffic leads to a continuous input of fine-grained serpentinite material into the accumulative strata of the sediment cascade. As a result, a pronounced effect of urban geochemical homogenization is realized in the regional ecology and geochemistry. This infrastructural influx of serpentinite dust not only obliterates local natural differences between cities but also acts as a macro-component matrix that partially masks conventional traffic-related trace element tracers (Cu, Sb, Zn). Furthermore, it is this pervasive road-induced homogenization that explains why the calculated background levels of Ni across all cities turned out to be higher than the global UCC crustal abundances.

sec.title: 4.4. Source-Specific Geochemical Flows and Tracers of Local Industrial Activities
sec.p: Certain media and elements within the eco-geochemical spectra reflect specific characteristics of pollutant input and transport. In monocities not associated with Cu smelting, the role of Sb emerges as a tracer of the period when coal was extensively utilized as fuel at power plants. The most illustrative example is Serov, where the transition to natural gas was implemented last. The systemic decrease in Sb content within current atmospheric deposition compared to other strata of the sediment cascade demonstrates the positive environmental effect of converting the energy sector to natural gas.

In Serov, lithophile Mn on one hand is tightly integrated into the shared cluster associations with toxic pollutants (Pb, Zn, Cd, Cu) within the snow cover, and on the other hand, exhibits high PI values across other strata of the sediment cascade. The anomalous behavior of Mn in Serov reflects the specifics of a full metallurgical cycle (including ferrochrome production and blast furnace smelting), where the volume of anthropogenic Mn emissions completely overwhelms and transforms the natural regional geochemical baseline. This conclusion also leads to the assumption that the elevated Mn PI values observed in the USDSs of Alapaevsk represent a legacy of its historical industrial period.

The capabilities of the proposed method in terms of identifying specific technogenic flows of individual elements are further illustrated by the case of Mg, which appeared in the snow cover of Serov due to the accidental emission. Although this element is not classified as toxic when bound within the soil and sediment matrix, it strictly requires regulatory monitoring within ambient air.

sec.title: 4.5. Toxicity-Weighted Assessment of Urban Environments Pollution
sec.p: Conventional assessment methods (including individual metrics such as the geoaccumulation index (Igeo), and enrichment factor or multi-element indicators like the Nemerow pollution index and the summary pollution indicator, Zc, adopted in the Russian Federation, possess a significant limitation: they evaluate the geochemical contrast of elements in isolation from their actual biological impact. In this study, an approach was proposed and tested based on the calculation of the TWPI. In this framework, the toxicological weight of each element (ranging from 2.7 for Mg to 55 for Pb and Cd) is strictly predetermined by its official hazard class according to the Russian state sanitary and hygienic standards for soils and ambient air. This methodology enables the verification of the actual quality of the urban environment.

The analysis of TWPI distribution across established ranges reveals a large-scale regional problem: in total, more than half of all surveyed residential areas in small- and medium-sized Ural cities fall into the heavy and severe toxic contamination categories. In Serov, this metric reaches an unprecedented 78% of the sampled sites.

The specific nature of environmental risks in the investigated region is exacerbated by two interconnected factors: the grain-size distribution of the sediments and the climatic regime of northern latitudes. The majority of toxic metal pollutants, particularly those of aerosol origin, are concentrated within the dust fraction of the deposits with a particle size of less than 0.1 mm, about 10% of which consists of a respirable fraction smaller than 10 μm [27]. Under the conditions of a prolonged winter period, these highly toxic fine-grained elements are accumulated within the structure of the snow cover. However, during the rapid spring melt, their acute release occurs. Initially, the toxicants enter the liquid and solid phases of the snow–dirt sludge on road surfaces. Subsequently, as the USDS dries out, the fine fraction undergoes secondary deflation. Consequently, the period after snow melting prior to the appearance of vegetative cover becomes a critical temporal window—the winter-accumulated toxic elements of hazard classes I and II are elevated into the surface atmospheric layer, directly into the human breathing zone. The developed TWPI matrix, relying on the surface sediment rather than soil, conclusively demonstrates that the population of Ural monocities is subjected to pronounced inhalation pressure during this period. This underscores the urgent need to revise municipal spring-cleaning regulations, shifting from dry sweeping to vacuum and hydro-flushing technologies to mitigate respiratory risks.

list-item.p: A comprehensive methodological approach has been developed and validated for assessing the environmental status of urban environments. This framework is based on sampling and analyzing heavy metals within the coupled accumulative media of an urban sediment cascade, encompassing soil, USDS, their fine dust fraction, and atmospheric deposition/snow. The approach integrates local geochemical baseline reconstruction, the calculation of geochemically justified PI, and the characterization of eco-geochemical spectra.

The multi-strata profiling approach enables the effective differentiation of historical environmental legacy footprints, the characterization of contemporary technogenic emissions, and the tracking of current trends in urban environmental transformation under changing meteorological conditions. Several key trajectories of technogenic transformation and ecological vulnerability have been identified and characterized across the investigated monocities: post-industrial legacy, continuous pressure from metallurgical complexes, mining impacts, and climate-dependent transboundary atmospheric transport.

The framework successfully isolates source-specific geochemical flows and tracers of local industrial activities. These markers capture specific facets of the technogenic transformation of the urban environment, including the dynamics of progressive environmental self-purification following the cessation of operations at individual pollution sources.

Traffic-related contamination is ubiquitous across all investigated cities, currently establishing PI values across various strata of the sediment cascade at a relatively uniform level regardless of the municipality. However, in the presence of powerful sources of contemporary industrial pollution, vehicular traffic can be classified as a secondary contributor to the overall contamination load.

Utilizing the toxicity-weighted pollution index, the actual environmental quality of the monocities was ranked, revealing a critical regional challenge: in total, more than half (54%) of the residential zones in the investigated mid- and small-sized cities fall into the heavy and severe toxic contamination categories, peaking at 78% of sampled sites in Serov. These findings underscore the urgent need to develop and implement effective, targeted environmental management systems and updated municipal cleaning regulations in industrial monocities.

The developed approach, based on the multi-strata profiling of urban sediment cascade combined with a toxicity-weighted matrix, provides a universally scalable methodology that transcends regional boundaries. This framework can be effectively adapted for multi-temporal environmental monitoring, quality of the urban environment assessment, and targeted urban management within industrial and post-industrial urban areas globally.
